title: Kavanah, intention
hook: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, the heart aimed at what the lips are saying

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hitbodedut: Rebbe Nachman's way of speaking to God in your own words, out loud, somewhere quiet. Your line was my own words.

Before they prayed, the pious ones of old would wait an hour. That's how the Mishnah, the collection of early Jewish law, describes them. Not to get the words ready. They knew the words. They waited to get the heart ready, to direct it toward their Father in heaven. Then the same passage turns strict. Once you've begun, even if a king greets you, don't answer him. Even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop. That's a great deal of attention for a few minutes of words.
screen: `THEY WAITED AN HOUR.` → `TO GET THE HEART READY.` → `NOT EVEN FOR A KING.`

segments.voice: The name for what they waited for is kavanah, usually translated intention, or directed intention: the heart aimed, the way you aim your steps down a road. The Mishnah uses this language of aiming; in one rule about reciting the Shema, the question is simply whether a person directed his heart. The roots reach into the Torah. Deuteronomy, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, asks Israel "to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." The rabbis of the Talmud asked a sharp question about that line: what kind of service happens in the heart? Their answer was prayer. So prayer is the service of the heart, and kavanah is what makes it the heart's. Then a tension Jewish teachers have turned over for a long time. Jewish prayer has fixed words, said at fixed times. The fixed part has its own name, keva. Kavanah is the living part. Lean only on keva and the words run on autopilot. Wait only for kavanah and you might never get around to praying. The Mishnah names the danger in one line: whoever makes their prayer a fixed task, their prayer is not a plea. Yet the tradition doesn't throw out the fixed words because the heart wanders. It keeps the words, and keeps asking for the aim. And the idea reaches past prayer: Jewish teachers speak of kavanah in eating, in giving, in the small commanded acts of an ordinary day.
screen: `KAVANAH: THE HEART, AIMED.` · `PRAYER, THE SERVICE OF THE HEART.` · `FIXED WORDS, LIVING AIM.` · `NOT ONLY IN PRAYER.` · then, large: `TO SERVE HIM WITH ALL YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Pick one small act you can do right now: a sip of water, folding your hands, standing up from your chair. Before you do it, wait one breath, the way the pious ones waited, and know what you're about to do and why; if you pray, point it toward God, and if you don't, toward the person or the day it serves. Then do it slowly, all the way through, and nothing else.
Kavanah. Directed intention: the heart aimed at what the lips or hands are doing, in Jewish prayer and beyond it. Today's word.
Your line: kavanah. The same act can be done with the heart pointed at it, or on the way to something else. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two, done.

howItsDone: Jews who pray the set daily prayers try to bring kavanah, directed intention, to the fixed words; teachers in the tradition also speak of bringing it to blessings, meals and other daily acts.

chat.says: If prayers use the same fixed words every day, how can they mean anything?
options: The words stay fixed; kavanah is aiming your heart at them each time you say them.
Kavanah means dropping the fixed words and praying only in your own words.
The meaning only comes if you wait a full hour first, like the pious ones.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 11:13: 'to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul'. The script names the translation as 'the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation'; that year is the translation's name, not a claim about the text.

Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 paraphrased: the pious ones of old (chasidim harishonim) waited an hour to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; even a king's greeting or a snake wound around the heel should not interrupt. The Talmud (Berakhot 32b-33a) limits the king case (e.g. a non-Jewish king, where there is danger); the script does not go into this. Confirm the fork's simplification is acceptable.
Mishnah Berakhot 2:1 (one reading the Torah when the time for the Shema arrives: 'if he directed his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation') is summarized loosely; confirm.
Taanit 2a: 'what is service of the heart? this is prayer' (on Deuteronomy 11:13), paraphrased.
Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 (Rabbi Eliezer: one who makes his prayer keva, his prayer is not supplication) paraphrased as 'a fixed task ... not a plea'; confirm.
Kavanah in eating, giving and mitzvot is stated generally as something 'Jewish teachers speak of'; the halakhic debate on whether mitzvot require intention (mitzvot tzrichot kavanah) is not entered.
